items.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018
items.q: one of the CDs I had out last night was the “Trayvon Martin Suite” thing that I did with Bill Cole

ctx.x: He had a political content to his music at times. And I wonder if you guys, if you feel any of your music has a political message.

All of our music has a political message. The thing is this: as African-American, especially African-American men, there’s always a message that we can do and we can survive. Because I can just leave here and go driving down across the Thruway and then you know get pulled over by a police officer and the next morning you read that I’ve been shot. And a lot of people won’t even bat their eye, because it’s just, this type of thing just happens. So the injustices that have been put on us as African-Americans, you…

people are failing to understand is because I say that Black Lives Matter, it doesn’t mean that other people’s lives do not matter, but they’re already protected in the system. You know, they’re not going to be shot down like Trayvon Martin for no reason or anything. They have these protections built in already. So people know their lives matter and they treat them with that type of respect. But for some strange reason, people, especially law enforcement and other people, think that our lives do not matter. So…
